01 / Introduction

Introduction and scope

Monte Carlo option pricing replaces an expectation that is difficult to evaluate with an average of simulated, discounted cash flows. Its usefulness comes from the contracts it can represent; its credibility comes from a careful account of uncertainty.

This guide develops simulation pricing from its probability foundations to practical estimators, variance reduction, path-dependent contracts and early exercise. The starting point is the risk-neutral pricing identity established in the Black–Scholes study guide. There, an analytical formula evaluates a particular expectation. Here, simulation evaluates that expectation numerically and then extends the calculation to payoffs for which an elementary formula is unavailable.

Three distinct objects

A model specifies the distribution of market variables. A contract specifies cash flows and the information available when decisions are made. An estimator specifies how simulated outcomes are combined into a price and an uncertainty estimate. Confusing these objects causes many implementation errors: an accurate simulation of the wrong measure prices the wrong expectation; an accurate simulation on the wrong monitoring schedule prices the wrong contract.

Under a specified model, the value V0V_0 is a number. A Monte Carlo estimate V^N\widehat V_N is a random variable whose realised value depends on the sample. The difference between these two is computational error. The difference between the model value and a traded price may also reflect calibration, liquidity, conventions and model inadequacy; it is not generally a Monte Carlo error.

Analogy: pricing a collection of lottery tickets. Imagine an option as a ticket with a payout determined by a future scenario. Simulate many correctly weighted scenarios, calculate what the ticket pays in each, and average the payouts after bringing them back to today. The simulated average estimates the ticket's value. The crucial qualification is “correctly weighted”: pricing weights are risk-neutral weights, not necessarily the frequencies an investor forecasts for the real world.

Reading structure and notation

Part I establishes expectations, estimators, uncertainty and simulation. Part II develops efficiency methods and contract-specific applications. Part III supplies a live laboratory, computed examples, implementation guidance, mathematical derivations and exercises with solutions. Basic probability, calculus and the idea of no-arbitrage pricing are assumed; the important formulas are derived rather than used as unexplained instructions.

Time starts at zero and maturity is TT, measured in years. Initial spot is S0S_0, strike is KK, continuously compounded interest rate is rr, continuous dividend yield is qq, and annualised volatility is σ\sigma. The symbol NN normally counts payoff evaluations; MM counts independent statistical units when these differ, as with antithetic pairs. The symbol mm counts time intervals or monitoring dates. All monetary values use one consistent currency unit.

Unless a caption specifies otherwise, examples use S0=K=100S_0=K=100, r=5%r=5%, q=0q=0, σ=20%\sigma=20% and T=1T=1. Figures are computed examples under stated models, not market observations. Hover over a plot to inspect values; multi-path plots display every path at the selected horizontal coordinate. The laboratory uses exact terminal GBM simulation and works offline.

02 / Valuation framework

Risk-neutral valuation and simulation

For a European terminal payoff HH, no-arbitrage valuation under a suitable risk-neutral measure ℚ\mathbb{Q} gives an expectation of discounted cash flows. With deterministic interest rates, the discount factor is known before any simulation is run:

V0=𝔼ℚ[D(0,T)H],D(0,T)=exp(−∫0Trsds).V_0=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[D(0,T)H],\qquad D(0,T)=\exp\left(-\int_0^T r_s\,ds\right).
(01)

For constant rr, write Y=e−rTHY=e^{-rT}H; pricing is the problem of estimating 𝔼ℚ[Y]\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[Y]. With several payments, add their separately discounted values within each scenario, then average the resulting scenario totals. This preserves the dependence between payments driven by the same market path.

Y=∑j=1JD(0,tj)Hj,V0=𝔼ℚ[Y].Y=\sum_{j=1}^{J}D(0,t_j)H_j,\qquad V_0=\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[Y].
(02)

Physical and pricing probabilities

Under the physical measure ℙ\mathbb{P}, the drift of an equity may reflect an expected return μ\mu. Under the money-market risk-neutral measure, a continuously dividend-paying stock with constant volatility instead follows

dSt=(r−q)Stdt+σStdWtℚ.dS_t=(r-q)S_t\,dt+\sigma S_t\,dW_t^{\mathbb{Q}}.
(03)

Substituting a bullish forecast for r−qr-q produces a forecast of an option's future payout under that forecast distribution. Discounting the result at rr does not turn it into the no-arbitrage price. Risk-neutral pricing does not assert that investors are actually indifferent to risk; it expresses the effect of replication and state prices in the chosen model.

A different numeraire changes both the pricing measure and the normalisation of the payoff. If AtA_t is a strictly positive tradable numeraire and ℚA\mathbb{Q}^{A} is its corresponding measure, the general identity is

V0=A0𝔼ℚA[HAT].V_0=A_0\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{A}}\left[\frac{H}{A_T}\right].
(04)

One cannot change a simulated drift while leaving the measure, discounting and payoff normalisation conceptually untouched. This becomes important in interest-rate models and forward-measure simulations. These notes use the money-market measure for the equity examples, with constant deterministic rates.

Terminal values, paths and exercise policies

A vanilla European payoff only needs STS_T. An Asian payoff also needs monitored averages. A barrier payoff needs a specified crossing event. A Bermudan payoff needs a stopping rule based on information available at its exercise dates. Simulation cost therefore depends on the information the contract requires, not on the visual appeal of drawing many paths.

With stochastic rates, D(0,T)=exp(−∫0Trsds)D(0,T)=\exp(-\int_0^T r_s\,ds) is itself random and belongs inside the simulated cash flow. Replacing it by the exponential of an average rate generally changes the expectation. Correlation between rates and the payoff also matters: a product of separate sample means does not estimate the expectation of their product.

The risk-neutral measure may not be uniquely determined by no-arbitrage in an incomplete market. A stochastic-volatility or jump model consequently requires additional choices and calibration. Monte Carlo is a numerical integration method once those choices are made; it does not resolve the underlying model-selection problem.

03 / Probability

Probability and statistical foundations

An expectation is a weighted average over a distribution, not an arithmetic average of arbitrarily selected scenarios. For a variable XX with density ff, a payoff transformation gg has expectation

𝔼[g(X)]=∫−∞∞g(x)f(x)dx.\mathbb{E}[g(X)]=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}g(x)f(x)\,dx.
(05)

Monte Carlo implements this weighting by drawing XiX_i from ff. A region with higher probability is visited more often. Uniformly spacing terminal stock prices and giving each one the same weight would instead approximate an integral against a uniform distribution over the selected range.

Independence, moments and covariance

The standard formulas below assume independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance. Independence means that knowing one observation does not change the distribution of another. Different simulated dates on one path are not independent; neither are two antithetic payoffs built from the same shock. Independent units must be identified before their uncertainty can be computed.

Var(Y)=𝔼[(Y−𝔼[Y])2],Cov(Y,C)=𝔼[(Y−𝔼[Y])(C−𝔼[C])].\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)=\mathbb{E}[(Y-\mathbb{E}[Y])(C-\mathbb{E}[C])].
(06)

Variance measures the spread of one discounted payoff. It has squared currency units. Standard deviation has currency units. Standard error measures the spread of a price estimator built from many observations. An option can have very volatile payoffs and still have a precisely estimated model price if enough appropriate simulations are available.

The law of large numbers

If the observations are IID and integrable, their average converges almost surely to the expectation. The theorem establishes the destination of the average; it does not promise a monotone approach, a particular error in one finite run, or a useful answer from a poorly sampled rare event.

1N∑i=1NYi⟶𝔼[Y]almost surely.\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_i\longrightarrow\mathbb{E}[Y]\quad\text{almost surely}.
(07)

Analogy: tasting a well-mixed soup. A spoonful samples the mixture; several spoonfuls give a better estimate of its average saltiness. Repeatedly sampling only the surface does not improve an estimate of the entire pot. In simulation, the sampling law and coverage of important payoff regions are the equivalent of correct mixing. Even correct sampling can miss a rare but consequential ingredient in a small sample.

The central limit theorem

With finite, nonzero variance σY2\sigma_Y^2, the centred sample average becomes approximately normal after the appropriate scaling:

N(V^N−V0)⇒N(0,σY2).\sqrt{N}(\widehat V_N-V_0)\Longrightarrow\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_Y^2).
(08)

This is an asymptotic statement about repeated samples. A severely skewed payoff, rare exercise or heavy-tailed likelihood weight may require far more observations before the approximation is useful. If a weighted estimator has infinite variance, the usual standard-error and normal-interval arguments are unavailable even when its expectation exists.

For GBM with fixed finite parameters, ordinary European call and put payoffs have finite moments of every positive order. That favourable property does not automatically carry over to every proposed importance-sampling scheme or every richer market model. The statistical assumptions belong to the resulting estimator, not simply to its method's name.

04 / Estimation

Monte Carlo estimators

Draw NN independent scenarios under the required measure, calculate their discounted payoffs YiY_i, and average them. The plain Monte Carlo estimator is

V^N=1N∑i=1NYi.\widehat V_N=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}Y_i.
(09)

Linearity of expectation makes this estimator unbiased when each payoff is sampled from the correct distribution and evaluated exactly. Independence is needed for the familiar variance formula, although unbiasedness itself only requires the correct marginal expectations.

𝔼[V^N]=V0,Var(V^N)=σY2N.\mathbb{E}[\widehat V_N]=V_0,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat V_N)=\frac{\sigma_Y^2}{N}.
(10)

What unbiasedness does and does not imply

Unbiasedness says that the average of estimates over repeated experiments equals the target. It does not say that a particular estimate equals the target, that most estimates lie on the same side, or that its distribution is symmetric at small sample sizes. A zero-payoff sample from a far out-of-the-money option can produce a zero estimate while the estimator remains unbiased across all possible samples.

A statistically unbiased estimator can still target the wrong model or contract. Exact simulation of monthly nodes, followed by node-only knock-out checks, is unbiased for a monthly-monitored barrier payoff. It generally overvalues the corresponding continuously monitored knock-out contract because crossings between nodes are omitted.

Online estimation and stable arithmetic

Storing every payoff is unnecessary for a price and sample variance. Welford's update accumulates the mean and a centred sum of squares without subtracting two nearly equal large totals. After observing YnY_n, let the current mean be ana_n and the centred sum be M2,nM_{2,n}:

an=an−1+Yn−an−1n,M2,n=M2,n−1+(Yn−an−1)(Yn−an).a_n=a_{n-1}+\frac{Y_n-a_{n-1}}{n},\qquad M_{2,n}=M_{2,n-1}+(Y_n-a_{n-1})(Y_n-a_n).
(11)

Start with zero count, mean and centred sum; after at least two observations, the sample variance is M2,n/(n−1)M_{2,n}/(n-1). Chunked processing can merge independent batches through their counts, means and centred sums. This keeps memory bounded and makes parallel aggregation explicit.

Conditional Monte Carlo

Sometimes one can integrate part of the randomness analytically. If G\mathcal{G} contains a subset of the simulated information, replacing a payoff by its conditional expectation preserves its mean:

𝔼[𝔼[Y|G]]=𝔼[Y],Var(𝔼[Y|G])≤Var(Y).\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}]]=\mathbb{E}[Y],\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid\mathcal{G}])\le\operatorname{Var}(Y).
(12)

The variance inequality follows from the law of total variance. Conditional averaging removes randomness that does not need to be sampled. Brownian-bridge survival weighting for barriers is an important example: conditional on monitored endpoints, average over the unresolved crossing event instead of drawing an additional crossing indicator.

Simulation should therefore be reserved for what remains difficult to integrate. Using an exact terminal distribution instead of Euler stepping, an analytical geometric-Asian control, or a conditional crossing probability is mathematical simplification before computational acceleration.

05 / Statistical uncertainty

Error analysis and confidence intervals

An estimate without a measure of its precision is incomplete. For NN IID discounted payoffs, estimate the one-payoff variance from deviations around their sample mean. The estimated standard error divides that standard deviation by the square root of the independent sample size:

sY2=1N−1∑i=1N(Yi−V^N)2,SE^(V^N)=sYN.s_Y^2=\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(Y_i-\widehat V_N)^2,\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat V_N)=\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt{N}}.
(13)

Discount first, then compute the sample variance, or consistently multiply an undiscounted payoff standard deviation by the deterministic discount factor. Mixing a discounted mean with an undiscounted standard error produces an incorrect interval. With random discount factors, their interaction with payoffs must be retained within every observation.

Approximate confidence intervals

A central-limit-theorem approximation produces a two-sided 100(1−α)%100(1-\alpha)\% interval using a standard normal quantile z1−α/2z_{1-\alpha/2}. At 95%, the commonly used quantile is approximately 1.96:

IN=[V^N−z1−α/2sYN,V^N+z1−α/2sYN].I_N=\left[\widehat V_N-z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt{N}},\ \widehat V_N+z_{1-\alpha/2}\frac{s_Y}{\sqrt{N}}\right].
(14)

The frequentist interpretation concerns the procedure: if the experiment were repeated independently, approximately 95% of intervals produced by a well-calibrated 95% procedure would contain the fixed model value. It does not assign a 95% probability to the already fixed model price conditional on one realised interval.

A Student tt quantile can replace the normal quantile when variance is estimated. The resulting interval is exact for IID normal observations; option payoffs are generally not normal, so using tt is not a universal small-sample repair. Skewness and rare events still matter. A bootstrap also cannot recover a payoff region absent from the observed sample.

Bias and mean squared error

Let VmV_m be the expectation of a payoff calculated on a discretised scheme. Its estimator may be unbiased for VmV_m while biased for the desired continuous-model value VV. The total error decomposes into a random sampling component and a systematic approximation component:

V^N,m−V=(V^N,m−Vm)+(Vm−V).\widehat V_{N,m}-V=(\widehat V_{N,m}-V_m)+(V_m-V).
(15)
MSE(V^N,m)=Var(Ym)N+(Vm−V)2.\operatorname{MSE}(\widehat V_{N,m})=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(Y_m)}{N}+(V_m-V)^2.
(16)

A narrow confidence interval estimates sampling uncertainty around the discretised target. It does not automatically include discretisation bias, an incorrect monitoring convention, policy approximation error or model risk. Reporting more decimal places also does not improve any of these errors.

Planning sample sizes

A pilot estimate sYs_Y gives an approximate production budget for a desired interval half-width ε\varepsilon:

N≈(z1−α/2sYε)2.N\approx\left(\frac{z_{1-\alpha/2}s_Y}{\varepsilon}\right)^2.
(17)

Round up, allow for uncertainty in the pilot variance and count independent units correctly. For an unbiased estimator, root mean squared error is σY/N\sigma_Y/\sqrt{N}; achieving a particular confidence half-width introduces the additional quantile. The two accuracy targets should not be silently interchanged.

Analogy: an instrument's repeatability and calibration. Repeating a measurement reduces noise from the instrument, but it does not correct a miscalibrated scale. More Monte Carlo observations reduce sampling error; refining the simulation scheme addresses numerical bias. Both require attention, but they require different experiments.

Rare payoffs and repeated monitoring

If every simulated payoff is zero, the usual sample variance and interval can both be zero. This is evidence of an uninformative sample, not proof that the price is zero. Inspect exercise counts, use a justified rare-event method, or increase the sample. For a binary event with zero successes in NN independent trials, a one-sided 95% binomial upper bound on its probability is 1−0.051/N1-0.05^{1/N}, approximately 3/N3/N. That bound is for a probability, not for the unbounded monetary payoff of a call.

Repeatedly checking a fixed-sample interval and stopping at the first attractive result changes the procedure's coverage. The running laboratory intervals are descriptive, pointwise intervals at their displayed sample sizes. A formally justified sequential stopping rule requires a sequential analysis or a confidence sequence; the entire displayed band is not a 95% simultaneous guarantee.

06 / Randomness

Random number generation and reproducibility

A numerical generator produces a reproducible stream of values that is used as an approximation to independent draws. A seed determines the initial state. Repeating a seed in the same implementation reproduces the calculation; repeating it does not provide a second independent experiment.

From uniforms to normal shocks

The inverse-transform method starts with an open-interval uniform variable UU and sets Z=Φ−1(U)Z=\Phi^{-1}(U). Normal shocks can also be generated in pairs by the Box–Muller transformation:

Z1=−2lnU1cos(2πU2),Z2=−2lnU1sin(2πU2).Z_1=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\cos(2\pi U_2),\qquad Z_2=\sqrt{-2\ln U_1}\sin(2\pi U_2).
(18)

The logarithm requires U1>0U_1>0. An inverse normal transform requires avoiding endpoints zero and one, which map to infinite shocks. Endpoint handling should be explicit; silently clipping a substantial tail region changes the distribution. Machine-level endpoint protection is different from deliberately truncating economically relevant tails.

The static experiments use NumPy generators with stated seeds. The browser laboratory uses a compact 32-bit Mulberry32 stream and Box–Muller normals for a reproducible teaching example. Its identical seed is reproducible within that implementation; it does not reproduce NumPy's different generator. A serious simulation system should choose and document an established generator, its version, state and parallel-stream policy.

Reproducibility and independence

Keep the seed, generator, parameter set, payoff definition, monitoring schedule and estimator settings together. Changing how draws are consumed can change results even with the same initial seed. For example, switching from terminal-only draws to a time-grid path changes which shocks drive each scenario.

Parallel jobs must not initialise every worker with the same seed. That duplicates paths and creates spurious apparent precision. Use a generator's supported stream-splitting, spawning or counter-based facility, and aggregate statistics over the genuinely distinct units. Merely observing different-looking worker outputs is not a stream-independence proof.

Common random numbers and moment matching

For controlled comparisons, reusing shocks is often desirable. When comparing two close parameter sets, common random numbers preserve path correspondence and can substantially reduce the variance of their difference. Independence between repetitions and deliberate dependence within a comparison serve different purposes.

One can recenter and rescale a finite normal sample so that its sample mean is zero and variance is one. This “moment matching” can reduce some errors, but it also makes the transformed shocks dependent. Standard IID variance formulas cannot be assumed without considering the modified estimator. It is not used in the live laboratory.

Useful diagnostics include sample moments, quantiles, tail counts, correlations and financial invariants. A sample mean near zero does not establish good high-dimensional behaviour. Conversely, a correct generator will exhibit ordinary sample deviations; forcing every diagnostic to its population value can obscure rather than validate the sampling design.

07 / Path simulation

Exact simulation of geometric Brownian motion

Constant-coefficient GBM is a particularly useful teaching model because its transition distribution is known exactly. Applying Itô's lemma to Xt=lnStX_t=\ln S_t turns the multiplicative stock diffusion into a drifted Brownian motion:

dXt=(r−q−12σ2)dt+σdWtℚ.dX_t=(r-q-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t^{\mathbb{Q}}.
(19)

Integrating over a time interval Δt\Delta t gives the exact transition. “Exact” refers to the model distribution at the selected dates; finite-precision arithmetic and finite-sample uncertainty still exist.

St+Δt=Stexp[(r−q−12σ2)Δt+σΔtZ],Z∼N(0,1).S_{t+\Delta t}=S_t\exp\left[(r-q-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)\Delta t+\sigma\sqrt{\Delta t}\,Z\right],\qquad Z\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).
(20)

Direct terminal sampling

For a terminal-only payoff, one shock per scenario suffices:

ST=S0exp[(r−q−12σ2)T+σTZ].S_T=S_0\exp\left[(r-q-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)T+\sigma\sqrt{T}\,Z\right].
(21)

Adding hundreds of intermediate dates cannot improve this exact terminal distribution. It increases work without removing any time-discretisation bias, because there was none in the first place. Path plots remain helpful for intuition, but the vanilla pricing algorithm does not need to retain those paths.

Path construction and dependence

For contract dates 0<t1<⋯<tm=T0<t_1<\cdots<t_m=T, draw independent normal increments and apply the transition on each interval. Stock levels on the same path are dependent because later levels include earlier shocks. With irregular dates, use each actual Δtj=tj−tj−1\Delta t_j=t_j-t_{j-1}; a uniform-grid approximation can change an averaging or exercise contract.

The lognormal moments provide useful checks. For any real aa with the expression finite,

𝔼ℚ[STa]=S0aexp[a(r−q)T+12a(a−1)σ2T].\mathbb{E}^{\mathbb{Q}}[S_T^a]=S_0^a\exp\left[a(r-q)T+\tfrac{1}{2}a(a-1)\sigma^2T\right].
(22)

In particular, 𝔼[ST]=S0e(r−q)T\mathbb{E}[S_T]=S_0e^{(r-q)T}. Thus the discounted stock has mean S0e−qTS_0e^{-qT}, which is the prepaid-forward value. With dividends, e−rtSte^{-rt}S_t alone is not the cumulative dividend-reinvested gain process; the yield adjustment in the expected discounted spot matters.

Boundary cases

If T=0T=0, the terminal stock is the current stock and the European price equals its immediate payoff. If σ=0\sigma=0, the risk-neutral path is deterministic: St=S0e(r−q)tS_t=S_0e^{(r-q)t}. Simulation is unnecessary in both cases. A negative interest rate is mathematically admissible in this constant-rate model and makes discount factors exceed one; a pricing routine should not reject it simply because it is negative.

GBM cannot represent negative prices, jumps, changing volatility or realistic volatility surfaces by itself. Its exact simulator is exact for this chosen model. Replacing it by a richer process requires revisiting transition sampling, numerical bias, calibration and payoff-specific error analysis.

08 / European options

European option valuation

A European call pays (ST−K)+(S_T-K)^+, where x+=max(x,0)x^+=\max(x,0); a put pays (K−ST)+(K-S_T)^+. Substituting the exact terminal distribution into these payoffs gives direct simulation estimators:

C^N=e−rTN∑i=1N(ST(i)−K)+,P^N=e−rTN∑i=1N(K−ST(i))+.\widehat C_N=\frac{e^{-rT}}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(S_T^{(i)}-K)^+,\qquad \widehat P_N=\frac{e^{-rT}}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}(K-S_T^{(i)})^+.
(23)

The same scenarios can estimate both options. Their estimates are then dependent, which is useful rather than problematic if the dependence is recognised. Pathwise, the call payoff minus the put payoff equals ST−KS_T-K. Averaging produces a particularly informative parity diagnostic:

C^N−P^N=e−rTS¯T−Ke−rT.\widehat C_N-\widehat P_N=e^{-rT}\overline S_T-Ke^{-rT}.
(24)

The finite-sample right-hand side contains the simulated stock mean. It generally differs from the population parity identity S0e−qT−Ke−rTS_0e^{-qT}-Ke^{-rT} by sampling noise. A sample-level discrepancy against that population identity should be assessed using the discounted-stock standard error, not interpreted immediately as a bug.

The analytical benchmark

Under the same constant-coefficient model, the exact prices are

C=S0e−qTΦ(d1)−Ke−rTΦ(d2),P=Ke−rTΦ(−d2)−S0e−qTΦ(−d1).C=S_0e^{-qT}\Phi(d_1)-Ke^{-rT}\Phi(d_2),\qquad P=Ke^{-rT}\Phi(-d_2)-S_0e^{-qT}\Phi(-d_1).
(25)
d1=ln(S0/K)+(r−q+12σ2)TσT,d2=d1−σT.d_1=\frac{\ln(S_0/K)+(r-q+\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T},\qquad d_2=d_1-\sigma\sqrt T.
(26)

These formulas are normally faster and more accurate for vanilla GBM options than Monte Carlo. Their role here is to supply known truth for estimator validation. A simulation that reproduces one call price is a useful first check; it does not validate every payoff, variance formula or early-exercise algorithm built later.

Exercise probability and payoff distribution

The probability that a call finishes in the money under ℚ\mathbb{Q} is Φ(d2)\Phi(d_2), not Φ(d1)\Phi(d_1). Many discounted payoffs can therefore be exactly zero. The remaining positive observations form a skewed right tail:

ℚ(ST>K)=Φ(d2),ℚ(Y=0)=Φ(−d2).\mathbb{Q}(S_T>K)=\Phi(d_2),\qquad \mathbb{Q}(Y=0)=\Phi(-d_2).
(27)

A histogram that treats zero observations as an ordinary continuous density conceals the atom at zero. The plotted distribution below states the zero mass separately and displays the positive-payoff density. Deep out-of-the-money options make that atom large, leaving a relatively small number of observations to estimate economically important tail contributions.

Digital contracts and nonlinearity

A cash-or-nothing digital call with cash amount AA has H=A𝟙ST>KH=A\mathbb{1}_{S_T>K} and exact price Ae−rTΦ(d2)Ae^{-rT}\Phi(d_2). Its payoff is discontinuous; this matters for Greek estimators and QMC smoothness. A call's price is not its exercise probability multiplied by a fixed expected stock gain unless the required conditional gain is also calculated.

Because a call payoff is convex, evaluating it at the expected stock price understates or equals the expected payoff: 𝔼[(ST−K)+]≥(𝔼[ST]−K)+\mathbb{E}[(S_T-K)^+]\ge(\mathbb{E}[S_T]-K)^+. Pricing the “average scenario” is therefore different from averaging scenario prices. This is one of the simplest reasons simulation must evaluate the payoff before taking the average.

09 / Convergence

Convergence and computational complexity

Plain Monte Carlo's characteristic rate is N−1/2N^{-1/2}. If the one-payoff standard deviation is unchanged, multiplying the sample size by four approximately halves the standard error; multiplying it by one hundred improves the standard error by a factor of ten. The rate is slow, even though the method is flexible.

SE(V^4N)=12SE(V^N),N=O(ε−2)for a fixed-variance unbiased estimator.\operatorname{SE}(\widehat V_{4N})=\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{SE}(\widehat V_N),\qquad N=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})\ \text{for a fixed-variance unbiased estimator}.
(28)

The sample-size exponent does not explicitly depend on the dimension of the random input. However, dimension can change payoff variance, the cost per path, correlation structures and the effectiveness of variance reduction. “Dimension independent convergence” should not be interpreted as constant computational cost for a thousand-factor contract.

Nested convergence traces

A running average uses increasingly long prefixes of one stream. Nearby estimates share most of their observations, so they are highly dependent. A smooth-looking running trace is not equivalent to many independent confirmations. Its apparent stability can also be misleading when a rare payoff region has not yet been visited.

A legitimate validation experiment repeats the entire calculation with independent streams, calculates the error against known truth, and examines root mean squared error and interval coverage. Such experiments should use a range of strikes and maturities; an at-the-money call is not a comprehensive tail-sampling test.

Cost-adjusted precision

Suppose one independent estimator unit has variance vv and average computational cost cc. With total budget BB, approximately B/cB/c units are affordable and the estimator variance is vc/Bvc/B. The efficiency criterion is therefore variance multiplied by cost:

Var(V^)≈vcB,efficiency comparison: vc.\operatorname{Var}(\widehat V)\approx\frac{vc}{B},\qquad \text{efficiency comparison: }vc.
(29)

An antithetic pair costs two payoff evaluations but contributes one independent average. A control method may require a pilot fit and an extra simulated control. A conditional method can add arithmetic while removing much more variance. Comparing methods at equal independent-unit counts can consequently misstate the computational benefit.

Practical stopping and reporting

Choose a precision target and an estimator before production sampling. A pilot can estimate the necessary budget; independent production avoids tuning on the same noise that is later reported. If a production budget is changed adaptively after repeated interval checks, the nominal fixed-sample coverage requires reconsideration.

Report the estimate, standard error, confidence construction, number of independent units, actual payoff evaluations and any pilot cost. Timing comparisons should include random-number generation, path construction, payoff evaluation and aggregation on the same hardware. A smaller standard error is useful, but a smaller standard error per second is the practical objective.

10 / Numerical approximation

Time discretisation and numerical bias

Exact transitions are not available for every stochastic model. For a diffusion dXt=a(Xt,t)dt+b(Xt,t)dWtdX_t=a(X_t,t)\,dt+b(X_t,t)\,dW_t, Euler–Maruyama approximates a short transition by freezing coefficients at the start of the interval:

Xj+1=Xj+a(Xj,tj)h+b(Xj,tj)hZj.X_{j+1}=X_j+a(X_j,t_j)h+b(X_j,t_j)\sqrt h\,Z_j.
(30)

For stock GBM this becomes Sj+1=Sj[1+(r−q)h+σhZj]S_{j+1}=S_j[1+(r-q)h+\sigma\sqrt h Z_j]. It can produce a negative stock, whereas GBM itself stays positive. The exact exponential transition is therefore preferable whenever its assumptions hold. Euler is shown here to explain discretisation error, not as an improvement over the exact GBM simulator.

Strong and weak errors

Strong error measures differences between coupled approximate and exact paths. Weak error measures differences in expectations of functionals. Under suitable regularity conditions, Euler commonly has strong order one half and weak order one; discontinuous payoffs and boundary events may change relevant rates.

(𝔼[|XTh−XT|2])1/2=O(h1/2),|𝔼[g(XTh)]−𝔼[g(XT)]|=O(h).\left(\mathbb{E}[|X_T^{h}-X_T|^2]\right)^{1/2}=\mathcal{O}(h^{1/2}),\qquad |\mathbb{E}[g(X_T^{h})]-\mathbb{E}[g(X_T)]|=\mathcal{O}(h).
(31)

These orders require assumptions; they are not universal warranties for any model, payoff or time step. A scheme can behave poorly if its coefficients grow rapidly, its states violate constraints or the contract is sensitive to crossings that the grid fails to resolve.

Milstein and path coupling

For a scalar diffusion, Milstein adds a correction involving the state derivative of the diffusion coefficient:

Xj+1=Xj+ajh+bjhZj+12bj∂xbjh(Zj2−1).X_{j+1}=X_j+a_jh+b_j\sqrt h Z_j+\tfrac{1}{2}b_j\,\partial_xb_j\,h(Z_j^2-1).
(32)

With appropriate scalar-model regularity it can improve strong order to one. In several dimensions, iterated stochastic integrals and noncommuting diffusion terms complicate the construction. Higher order is not automatically cheaper per unit of total pricing accuracy.

To estimate numerical bias efficiently, simulate coarse and fine paths with common Brownian increments. A coarse increment is the sum of its corresponding fine increments. Independent grids waste the strong relationship between two approximations to the same underlying path and make their expected difference harder to estimate.

Balancing sample size and mesh size

If bias is proportional to hαh^\alpha, allocate part of a total error budget to bias and part to sampling variance. With ordinary path simulation, per-path cost often scales as h−1h^{-1}. Achieving RMSE ε\varepsilon can then cost on the order of ε−2−1/α\varepsilon^{-2-1/\alpha}, rather than the terminal-only ε−2\varepsilon^{-2} rate.

A finer grid does not change a contract's explicitly discrete monitoring schedule. For an Asian option monitored at twelve fixed dates, exact simulation at those dates directly represents the contract. Extra non-fixing dates are not extra terms in its average. For a continuous barrier, however, unobserved crossings are part of the requested payoff and require a crossing correction or an appropriate limiting argument.

11 / Variance reduction

Antithetic variates

For symmetric normal inputs, simulate a payoff using ZZ and a companion using −Z-Z. Each marginal input has the correct distribution, so their average has the same expectation as either payoff. Repeat this construction using independent base shocks.

Ai=Y(Zi)+Y(−Zi)2,V^AV=1M∑i=1MAi,N=2M.A_i=\frac{Y(Z_i)+Y(-Z_i)}{2},\qquad \widehat V_{\mathrm{AV}}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M}A_i,\qquad N=2M.
(33)

The two members of one pair are deliberately dependent; the MM pair averages are the independent statistical units. Their variance determines the standard error:

Var(A)=12Var(Y)(1+ρ),SE^(V^AV)=sAM.\operatorname{Var}(A)=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1+\rho),\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\widehat V_{\mathrm{AV}})=\frac{s_A}{\sqrt M}.
(34)

Here ρ\rho is the correlation between the paired payoffs and the equality assumes their identical marginal variance. At equal payoff-evaluation budget N=2MN=2M, the estimator variance relative to plain Monte Carlo is 1+ρ1+\rho. Negative correlation creates a benefit; zero correlation creates no variance benefit per payoff evaluation.

Why it often works for vanilla options

The European call payoff increases with a terminal normal shock. Reversing the shock tends to turn a favourable call scenario into an unfavourable one. A put decreases with that shock, and the same reversal again counterbalances outcomes. The resulting averages tend to fluctuate less than separate unpaired payoffs.

Analogy: balancing opposite perturbations. If a measurement is distorted by a small upward perturbation in one trial, repeat it with the opposite perturbation and average. The perturbation's effects partly cancel. A nonlinear payoff does not cancel perfectly, and the useful cancellation depends on how the payoff responds to the perturbation.

Limits and implementation

A symmetric but nonmonotone payoff can produce positive paired correlation. Barrier and early-exercise features can also make the response complicated. Antithetic sampling is therefore a design to measure, not a universally beneficial switch.

For a multi-date GBM path, reverse the entire vector of Brownian shocks to construct the partner. Do not reverse independent shocks inconsistently across dates if the intended partner is a full sign reversal. For correlated assets, reverse the underlying independent normal vector; its correlated transformation is also reversed.

Store or stream pair averages for statistics. Calculating a standard error from all 2M2M dependent payoffs as if they were IID is incorrect. If an odd payoff budget is requested, specify how an unpaired observation is weighted; the live laboratory instead requires even budgets for antithetic methods to keep both cost and uncertainty transparent.

12 / Variance reduction

Control variates

A control variate is a simulated quantity CC with known expectation μC\mu_C that shares important variation with the target payoff YY. Subtracting its centred deviation leaves the target mean unchanged for a fixed coefficient β\beta:

YCV=Y−β(C−μC),V^CV=Y¯−β(C¯−μC).Y^{\mathrm{CV}}=Y-\beta(C-\mu_C),\qquad \widehat V_{\mathrm{CV}}=\overline Y-\beta(\overline C-\mu_C).
(35)

Expanding the variance and differentiating with respect to β\beta gives the population-optimal scalar coefficient and its residual variance:

β⋆=Cov(Y,C)Var(C),Var(YCV)=Var(Y)(1−ρYC2).\beta^\star=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Y,C)}{\operatorname{Var}(C)},\qquad \operatorname{Var}(Y^{\mathrm{CV}})=\operatorname{Var}(Y)(1-\rho_{YC}^2).
(36)

A strong positive or negative correlation is useful; the sign of the optimal coefficient adjusts accordingly. A control with zero variance is not informative for this optimisation and must not trigger a division by zero. Multiple controls generalise the coefficient to a covariance linear system, which should be solved stably rather than explicitly inverted.

Discounted stock as a vanilla control

For terminal GBM equity options, choose C=e−rTSTC=e^{-rT}S_T. Its known mean is S0e−qTS_0e^{-qT}. A high stock outcome increases a call's discounted payoff and the discounted stock together, allowing their shared movement to be removed.

The controlled observations need not be nonnegative even when the original option payoff is. Clipping negative observations or clipping a negative final estimate to zero changes the estimator and can introduce bias. No-arbitrage price bounds are population properties, not a licence to alter noisy observations without analysing the effect.

Analogy: removing a known background signal. Suppose a sensor records the target plus a background fluctuation. A second sensor observes a closely related background whose average level is known. Subtract its deviation from that known level, rather than its entire value. The shared noise decreases while the target's average is preserved.

Estimating coefficients without hidden optimism

A fitted coefficient from the same sample is random and correlated with its sample control mean. The resulting estimator is generally not exactly unbiased in finite samples. Residual sample variance alone can also underrepresent fitting effects. A clean construction estimates β\beta on an independent pilot, freezes it, and evaluates controlled payoffs on an independent production sample.

Conditional on the pilot, the frozen-coefficient production estimator is unbiased for the target. Its production standard error is calculated from adjusted observations. Cross-fitting offers another construction: fit on separate folds and apply each fit to held-out observations, with uncertainty calculations that respect the design.

Combining controls and antithetics

For antithetic simulation, control the pair averages AiA_i with the corresponding stock pair averages. The optimal coefficient for these averages differs from the optimal coefficient for individual payoffs. Pilot and production units must both follow the actual paired design.

A geometric-average payoff is a strong control for an arithmetic Asian payoff. A geometric basket can control an arithmetic basket under a lognormal multivariate model. A known European payoff can help estimate an early-exercise premium. In every case, the control expectation must match the simulated quantity exactly, including yield, discounting, maturity and monitoring convention.

13 / Sampling design

Stratified sampling and Latin hypercube

Partition the sample space into disjoint strata with known probabilities php_h. Sample within each stratum from its conditional distribution, estimate the stratum mean, and combine these means using their probability weights. This avoids relying on accidental sample proportions to represent every important region.

V^strat=∑h=1HphY¯h,Var(V^strat)=∑h=1Hph2σh2nh.\widehat V_{\mathrm{strat}}=\sum_{h=1}^{H}p_h\overline Y_h,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\widehat V_{\mathrm{strat}})=\sum_{h=1}^{H}\frac{p_h^2\sigma_h^2}{n_h}.
(37)

The variance expression assumes independence between stratum samples. With proportional allocation nh≈Nphn_h\approx Np_h, removing random variation in the number of observations allocated to each stratum reduces the between-stratum component of variance. The remaining uncertainty comes from variation within strata.

Allocation by variability and cost

Minimising variance at a fixed total sample size gives Neyman allocation, nh∝phσhn_h\propto p_h\sigma_h. If one observation in stratum hh costs chc_h, the cost-constrained allocation instead satisfies

nh∝phσhch.n_h\propto\frac{p_h\sigma_h}{\sqrt{c_h}}.
(38)

Stratum variances must usually be estimated from a pilot. Rounding and minimum sample counts require attention, especially for small strata where a within-stratum variance cannot be estimated from one observation. Known deterministic strata can be integrated exactly instead of simulated.

A normal-input example

For a terminal vanilla option, stratify U=Φ(Z)U=\Phi(Z) into equal-probability intervals. In each selected interval ((h−1)/H,h/H)((h-1)/H,h/H), draw a conditional uniform value, transform it with Φ−1\Phi^{-1}, and evaluate the discounted payoff. The weighting belongs to the probability interval, not its corresponding stock-price width.

A useful design gives explicit attention to the exercise threshold and the payoff tail. Strata with similar probability need not have similar contribution or variance: a rare high-stock stratum can contribute large call payoffs. Good allocation addresses this variation without changing the probability weights.

Latin hypercube designs

Latin hypercube sampling stratifies every marginal uniform coordinate. For NN points, independently permute stratum indices in each coordinate and draw one random point within each assigned interval:

Ui,j=πj(i)−1+Vi,jN,Vi,j∼Uniform(0,1).U_{i,j}=\frac{\pi_j(i)-1+V_{i,j}}{N},\qquad V_{i,j}\sim\operatorname{Uniform}(0,1).
(39)

Each coordinate covers all its one-dimensional strata, but the resulting NN multivariate points are dependent. The design can be effective when much of the integrand's variation comes from low-order marginal effects; arbitrary interactions and discontinuities may weaken its benefit. Coordinatewise stratification does not mean that every small multivariate cell receives an observation.

For correlated assets, build the design in independent-normal coordinates, then apply the desired correlation transformation. To quantify uncertainty robustly, repeat the entire randomised design independently and estimate variance across design means. Using the ordinary IID observation variance within one Latin hypercube without analysing its dependence is not a generally valid standard-error calculation.

14 / Rare-event simulation

Importance sampling and rare events

Plain simulation may spend most of its time on scenarios with zero payoff. Importance sampling draws more often from consequential regions, then uses a density ratio to preserve the original expectation. If ff is the target density and gg is the proposal density,

V=∫h(x)f(x)dx=𝔼g[h(X)f(X)g(X)].V=\int h(x)f(x)\,dx=\mathbb{E}_g\left[h(X)\frac{f(X)}{g(X)}\right].
(40)

The proposal must assign positive density wherever the target's relevant payoff contribution is nonzero. The statistical units are the weighted payoffs h(Xi)f(Xi)/g(Xi)h(X_i)f(X_i)/g(X_i), and their variance determines the standard error. Sample weights alone do not determine price uncertainty.

Exponential tilting of a normal shock

For a GBM terminal payoff, use a proposal Z∼N(θ,1)Z\sim\mathcal{N}(\theta,1) instead of the target N(0,1)\mathcal{N}(0,1). Cancelling the two normal densities yields an exact weight:

w(Z)=φ(Z)φ(Z−θ)=exp(−θZ+12θ2).w(Z)=\frac{\phi(Z)}{\phi(Z-\theta)}=\exp(-\theta Z+\tfrac{1}{2}\theta^2).
(41)

For a deep out-of-the-money call, a positive θ\theta makes exercise more frequent. The exercise threshold in normal coordinates provides a starting proposal location:

zK=ln(K/S0)−(r−q−12σ2)TσT.z_K=\frac{\ln(K/S_0)-(r-q-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2)T}{\sigma\sqrt T}.
(42)

Choosing θ=zK\theta=z_K is a transparent illustrative design, not the universally variance-minimising proposal. The best shift depends on the payoff size across the tail, not only on the exercise event. A pilot or a carefully derived optimisation can improve it.

Analogy: interviewing more people from a rare group. A survey can deliberately recruit more members of a rare group to learn about it. To estimate the whole population's average, the answers must be weighted back to the group's true prevalence. A proposal distribution likewise changes which scenarios are observed, while likelihood weights restore the required pricing average.

Weight instability and support

A poor proposal can increase variance dramatically. Some observations then carry enormous weights, dominating the estimate and undermining a normal confidence approximation. Examine weighted-payoff contributions, tail behaviour and independent-run stability; an attractive exercise count does not by itself establish an efficient estimator.

The often used weight diagnostic (∑iwi)2/∑iwi2(\sum_i w_i)^2/\sum_i w_i^2 measures concentration of weights, but it is not a universal effective sample size for the option price. Payoff–weight dependence also matters. For ordinary importance sampling with known normalised densities, use the average of weighted payoffs. Dividing by the realised sum of weights creates a self-normalised estimator, which is generally biased at finite sample sizes.

For a nonnegative integrand, an ideal zero-variance proposal is proportional to h(x)f(x)h(x)f(x). Its normalising constant is the unknown target value, so it is generally a theoretical guide rather than an executable solution. Practical proposals approximate important payoff regions while keeping all likelihood calculations correct.

15 / Low-discrepancy integration

Quasi-Monte Carlo methods

Express the price as an integral over independent uniforms on the unit cube. Transform each coordinate to the required random input and evaluate the discounted contract payoff:

V=∫[0,1]df(u)du,V^QMC=1N∑i=1Nf(ui).V=\int_{[0,1]^d}f(u)\,du,\qquad \widehat V_{\mathrm{QMC}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}f(u_i).
(43)

Quasi-Monte Carlo replaces unstructured random points with a low-discrepancy design, such as a Sobol sequence. Its points cover the integration domain more evenly according to particular geometric criteria. The goal is smaller integration error, not a closer resemblance to visually random paths.

Deterministic and randomised designs

A deterministic point set does not supply IID observations. Its ordinary sample payoff variance divided by NN is not a justified Monte Carlo standard error. Mathematical discrepancy bounds require assumptions about variation and can be uninformative for singular inverse-normal transformations or discontinuous payoffs.

Randomised QMC introduces a randomisation that preserves the design's structure and the needed marginal uniformity. Independently scramble the whole design RR times, calculate one price estimate per scramble, and use those price estimates as the independent units for uncertainty:

V¯R=1R∑r=1RV^(r),SE^(V¯R)=1R(R−1)∑r=1R(V^(r)−V¯R)2.\overline V_R=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\widehat V^{(r)},\qquad \widehat{\operatorname{SE}}(\overline V_R)=\sqrt{\frac{1}{R(R-1)}\sum_{r=1}^{R}(\widehat V^{(r)}-\overline V_R)^2}.
(44)

A tt-based interval across scramble means is often useful, but its calibration still depends on the number and distribution of independent means. This construction measures the error of their average; it should not be presented as the standard error of an individual scramble.

Effective dimension and Brownian ordering

A path may use hundreds of normal coordinates while most payoff variation is driven by a few broad features. Effective dimension describes how strongly those coordinates or low-order interactions contribute. Assigning influential directions to early, well-covered QMC coordinates can improve performance.

A Brownian-bridge construction samples the terminal Brownian value first, then intermediate values conditionally. Principal-component constructions similarly concentrate much covariance variation into leading directions. Both preserve the Brownian distribution when implemented correctly; they change which independent coordinates explain large-scale path variation.

This Brownian-bridge construction is distinct from using bridge crossing probabilities to correct barrier monitoring. One is an ordering of Gaussian path generation; the other integrates unobserved crossing events conditional on endpoints. They can be combined, but they solve different problems.

Sequence conventions

Sobol balance properties are tied to suitable sample sizes, notably powers of two in the implementation used here. Arbitrarily thinning a sequence or dropping its first point can damage those properties. The computed experiment uses SciPy's scrambled Sobol engine and complete 2m2^m-point designs; separate scramble seeds supply independent repetitions. See the implementation reference for the precise construction.

The empirical advantage in the figure is especially favourable because the vanilla example is one-dimensional. A nonsmooth high-dimensional contract may behave differently. Report realised performance and uncertainty for the actual payoff instead of promising an N−1N^{-1} rate for every application.

16 / Multilevel estimation

Multilevel Monte Carlo

When a fine path approximation is expensive, multilevel Monte Carlo estimates its expectation through a hierarchy of cheaper approximations and strongly coupled corrections. Let PℓP_\ell be a discounted payoff at mesh hℓ=2−ℓTh_\ell=2^{-\ell}T. A telescoping identity decomposes the finest expectation exactly:

𝔼[PL]=𝔼[P0]+∑ℓ=1L𝔼[Pℓ−Pℓ−1].\mathbb{E}[P_L]=\mathbb{E}[P_0]+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\mathbb{E}[P_\ell-P_{\ell-1}].
(45)

Most of the value can be estimated with many cheap coarse samples. Fewer expensive samples estimate fine-minus-coarse corrections, provided those corrections have small variance. Fine and coarse payoffs in a correction must share the same underlying Brownian path: each coarse increment sums its associated fine increments.

V^ML=1N0∑iP0(i)+∑ℓ=1L1Nℓ∑i(Pℓ(i)−Pℓ−1(i)).\widehat V_{\mathrm{ML}}=\frac{1}{N_0}\sum_iP_0^{(i)}+\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\frac{1}{N_\ell}\sum_i(P_\ell^{(i)}-P_{\ell-1}^{(i)}).
(46)

Different levels can use independent samples; within each correction, coupling is essential. With independent fine and coarse simulations, the correction variance can remain comparable to the payoff variance instead of shrinking with the mesh.

Analogy: a rough map plus local corrections. It is cheaper to build a broad map at low resolution and use detailed surveys to correct its missing features than to survey every location at maximum resolution. The detailed surveys must refer to the same locations as the rough map; otherwise their differences include unrelated variation.

Allocating work

Let VℓV_\ell be correction variance and CℓC_\ell its per-sample cost. Minimising total cost subject to a sampling-variance target vtargetv_{\mathrm{target}} gives an approximate allocation

Nℓ≈1vtargetVℓCℓ∑k=0LVkCk.N_\ell\approx\frac{1}{v_{\mathrm{target}}}\sqrt{\frac{V_\ell}{C_\ell}}\sum_{k=0}^{L}\sqrt{V_kC_k}.
(47)

Estimate variances and costs in a pilot, round allocations up and monitor whether the finest level's remaining bias meets its separate budget. The telescoping identity targets 𝔼[PL]\mathbb{E}[P_L], not automatically the continuous-model expectation.

Complexity under explicit rate assumptions

Suppose bias decays as 2−αL2^{-\alpha L}, correction variance as 2−βℓ2^{-\beta\ell}, and cost per correction as 2γℓ2^{\gamma\ell}, with the regularity and allocation conditions required by the multilevel theorem, including α≥12min(β,γ)\alpha\ge\frac12\min(\beta,\gamma). The leading cost to reach RMSE ε\varepsilon has the following orders:

Multilevel cost regimes under the stated asymptotic assumptions
Variance versus cost growthCost order
β>γ\beta>\gammaO(ε−2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})
β=γ\beta=\gammaO(ε−2(logε)2)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2}(\log\varepsilon)^2)
β<γ\beta<\gammaO(ε−2−(γ−β)/α)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-2-(\gamma-\beta)/\alpha})

For many Euler diffusion examples, α=1\alpha=1, β=1\beta=1, γ=1\gamma=1, giving a substantial improvement over single-level grid simulation. Discontinuous or path-dependent functionals may require specialised coupling or smoothing. Exact terminal GBM sampling remains simpler for the vanilla benchmark; using MLMC there would create an unnecessary approximation hierarchy. The method's value appears when such exact simplification is unavailable.

17 / Multiple assets

Correlated assets and basket options

A multi-asset payoff depends on the joint distribution, not just the individual distributions. For constant-coefficient correlated GBM, terminal log prices satisfy

lnSi,T=lnSi,0+(r−qi−12σi2)T+σiTZi,𝔼[ZiZj]=ρij.\ln S_{i,T}=\ln S_{i,0}+(r-q_i-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_i^2)T+\sigma_i\sqrt T\,Z_i,\qquad \mathbb{E}[Z_iZ_j]=\rho_{ij}.
(48)

Build the correlation matrix RR, factor it as R=LLTR=LL^\mathsf{T}, draw an independent standard-normal vector UU, and set Z=LUZ=LU. Since Cov(U)=I\operatorname{Cov}(U)=I, the transformed covariance is LLT=RLL^\mathsf{T}=R. Every path needs a new independent base vector; its asset coordinates are intentionally dependent after transformation.

Admissible correlation matrices

A matrix with ones on the diagonal and pairwise entries between minus one and one is not necessarily a valid correlation matrix. It must also be symmetric and positive semidefinite. Cholesky factorisation generally requires positive definiteness; a valid singular matrix can instead use an eigenvalue factorisation restricted to its nonnegative modes.

Small negative eigenvalues from numerical roundoff can be handled with a documented tolerance. A materially indefinite matrix is a modelling error; silently taking absolute eigenvalues changes the supplied dependence structure. For dd equal pairwise correlations, admissibility requires −1/(d−1)≤ρ≤1-1/(d-1)\le\rho\le1. The three-asset example stays inside that range.

Arithmetic and geometric baskets

An arithmetic basket call with nonnegative weights summing to one pays (∑iwiSi,T−K)+(\sum_i w_iS_{i,T}-K)^+. Its constituent lognormal variables do not make their arithmetic sum lognormal. Monte Carlo directly evaluates the actual sum without imposing a lognormal approximation.

Vbasket=e−rT𝔼[(∑i=1dwiSi,T−K)+].V_{\mathrm{basket}}=e^{-rT}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}w_iS_{i,T}-K\right)^+\right].
(49)

A geometric basket GT=∏iSi,TwiG_T=\prod_i S_{i,T}^{w_i} has a normally distributed logarithm under this model. Its parameters are

μG=∑iwi[lnSi,0+(r−qi−12σi2)T],vG=T∑i∑jwiwjσiσjρij.\mu_G=\sum_iw_i\left[\ln S_{i,0}+(r-q_i-\tfrac{1}{2}\sigma_i^2)T\right],\qquad v_G=T\sum_i\sum_jw_iw_j\sigma_i\sigma_j\rho_{ij}.
(50)

The geometric-basket call therefore has an analytical lognormal price and can serve as a control for the arithmetic-basket call. Controls built from individual discounted stocks are also available. With nonnegative normalised weights, the arithmetic basket exceeds or equals the geometric basket pathwise; their call values inherit that ordering when all other contract conventions agree.

Interpretation and extensions

Changing correlation changes how much the assets offset or reinforce each other in a basket. The plotted example shows increasing call value as its equal-correlation parameter increases. This observation is tied to the displayed weights, marginal models and convex payoff; it should not be extrapolated indiscriminately to a spread, a minimum option or a barrier on several assets.

Historical correlation is not automatically the appropriate calibrated pricing dependence. Under stochastic volatility, jumps or heavy-tailed copulas, the joint model requires further specification. Higher dimensions also increase path cost and can reduce the effectiveness of sampling schemes; dimensional flexibility does not remove the need to validate the joint distribution.

18 / Path dependence

Asian and other path-dependent options

An arithmetic Asian option averages observed stock prices before applying its payoff. For equally weighted dates tjt_j, the fixed-strike call has

A=1m∑j=1mStj,H=(A−K)+,V=e−rT𝔼[H].A=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{j=1}^{m}S_{t_j},\qquad H=(A-K)^+,\qquad V=e^{-rT}\mathbb{E}[H].
(51)

The averaging operation precedes the nonlinear payoff. Averaging vanilla call payoffs over dates produces a different contract. Including the initial spot, using irregular weights, or paying at a date different from the final fixing also changes the cash flow and must be specified.

A geometric-average control

Define the geometric average on exactly the same dates. Its logarithm is an average of jointly normal log prices, so it is normal. Writing a=r−q−σ2/2a=r-q-\sigma^2/2, its mean and variance are

G=exp(1m∑jlnStj),μG=lnS0+am∑jtj,vG=σ2m2∑i∑jmin(ti,tj).G=\exp\left(\frac{1}{m}\sum_j\ln S_{t_j}\right),\qquad \mu_G=\ln S_0+\frac{a}{m}\sum_jt_j,\qquad v_G=\frac{\sigma^2}{m^2}\sum_i\sum_j\min(t_i,t_j).
(52)

For fixings tj=jT/mt_j=jT/m, excluding the initial spot, these simplify to

μG=lnS0+aTm+12m,vG=σ2T(m+1)(2m+1)6m2.\mu_G=\ln S_0+aT\frac{m+1}{2m},\qquad v_G=\sigma^2T\frac{(m+1)(2m+1)}{6m^2}.
(53)

A lognormal payoff expectation then gives the exact geometric-Asian call price:

CG=e−rT[eμG+vG/2Φ(dG+vG)−KΦ(dG)],dG=μG−lnKvG.C_G=e^{-rT}\left[e^{\mu_G+v_G/2}\Phi(d_G+\sqrt{v_G})-K\Phi(d_G)\right],\qquad d_G=\frac{\mu_G-\ln K}{\sqrt{v_G}}.
(54)

Use e−rT(G−K)+e^{-rT}(G-K)^+ as the control and CGC_G as its known expectation. Arithmetic and geometric averages tend to move together, so this removes a large portion of payoff variation. The coefficient should be fitted on a separate pilot or treated with an appropriate alternative statistical design.

Analogy: comparing two almost identical thermometers. One thermometer is the difficult arithmetic payoff; the other is the closely related geometric payoff whose average reading is known exactly. Their shared deviations can be removed. The closer their scenario responses, the more precise the remaining difference becomes.

Discrete and continuous averaging

For a continuously monitored geometric average, lnG=T−1∫0TlnStdt\ln G=T^{-1}\int_0^T\ln S_t\,dt has mean lnS0+aT/2\ln S_0+aT/2 and variance σ2T/3\sigma^2T/3. These are limits of the displayed discrete parameters. A continuously averaged geometric formula is not an exact control expectation for an average observed on only twelve dates.

A numerical grid used to approximate a continuously averaged arithmetic contract creates integration bias. Increasing the number of fixing dates in an explicitly discrete contract instead changes the contract. The figure compares different stated discrete schedules and does not describe those prices as numerical errors around a single twelve-fixing contract.

Other path functionals

Lookback payoffs depend on a maximum or minimum; cliquets aggregate local returns, often with caps and floors; realised-variance contracts depend on a prescribed return statistic. For each, determine which state variables can be accumulated online and which crossing or extrema information is unresolved by the grid. Running sums, extrema and realised-return totals often eliminate the need to retain a full path.

Path dependence can make simulation useful even in a simple market model. It also makes contract conventions more important: observation calendars, fixing weights, treatment of the initial observation and settlement timing must match between the payoff, control and reference calculation.

19 / Barrier monitoring

Barrier options and Brownian bridges

An up-and-out call with upper barrier B>S0B>S_0 and no rebate pays a vanilla call only if the stock never reaches BB during the monitoring period. For continuous monitoring, its payoff is

H=(ST−K)+𝟙max0≤t≤TSt<B.H=(S_T-K)^+\mathbb{1}_{\max_{0\le t\le T}S_t<B}.
(55)

A grid check sees only its nodes. A stock can cross the barrier and return below it between two observations. Ignoring that event overstates survival and generally overprices a continuously monitored knock-out. Exact lognormal endpoint sampling does not solve this missing-path-information problem by itself.

Conditional crossing probabilities

Under constant-volatility GBM, log spot is a Brownian motion with constant drift. Conditional on two log endpoints xj,xj+1x_j,x_{j+1} below b=lnBb=\ln B, the probability of an upper-barrier crossing within an interval hh is

pj=exp[−2(b−xj)(b−xj+1)σ2h].p_j=\exp\left[-\frac{2(b-x_j)(b-x_{j+1})}{\sigma^2h}\right].
(56)

The drift cancels after conditioning on endpoints. If either endpoint reaches or exceeds the barrier, survival is zero. Conditional bridges on separate intervals are independent given the grid values, allowing their interval survival probabilities to be multiplied.

Ybridge=e−rT(ST−K)+∏j=0m−1(1−pj),Y_{\mathrm{bridge}}=e^{-rT}(S_T-K)^+\prod_{j=0}^{m-1}(1-p_j),
(57)

with the product set to zero for any barrier-breaching endpoint. This weighted payoff integrates over the unobserved crossing indicators. Under the stated constant-coefficient GBM assumptions, it targets the continuously monitored value without node-monitoring bias. It is not a general exact formula for arbitrary stochastic volatility, moving barriers, double barriers or additional path-dependent cash flows.

A useful terminal-only simplification

For this particular upper barrier and terminal vanilla payoff, conditioning only on the terminal stock is already sufficient. A single Brownian bridge spanning the whole life supplies the survival probability. Thus the continuous-monitoring price can be computed by a one-dimensional integral of the terminal payoff times that probability. The horizontal reference in the figure uses numerical quadrature of this conditional expectation.

This is a stronger simplification than adding more dates. More monitored endpoints can increase conditional-payoff variance because they reveal more information about survival. They may still be required by a more complicated contract; their benefit should follow from that contract rather than from an assumption that more nodes always improve every estimator.

Discrete monitoring and rebates

If a contract explicitly monitors only specified closing prices, crossings between those dates do not knock it out. Applying continuous bridge survival weights would price a different contract. Continuity corrections that approximate the relation between discrete and continuous barriers are also different from directly integrating conditional crossings.

Rebates paid immediately at first passage depend on the hitting time and its discount factor. Simply adding a fixed maturity-discounted rebate to a survival-weighted terminal payoff does not represent an immediate rebate. Likewise, knock-in/out parity requires matching the same barrier event, payoff and rebate convention on both sides.

20 / Greeks

Monte Carlo sensitivity estimation

A Greek is a derivative of the model expectation with respect to an input. It has its own estimator, standard error and numerical assumptions. A precise price estimate does not automatically imply a precise delta or gamma estimate.

Finite differences and common random numbers

A central spot difference approximates delta by repricing at two perturbed spots:

Δ^h=V^(S0+h)−V^(S0−h)2h.\widehat\Delta_h=\frac{\widehat V(S_0+h)-\widehat V(S_0-h)}{2h}.
(58)

For a sufficiently smooth price function its deterministic truncation bias is of order h2h^2. With independent simulation errors in the two prices, dividing their difference by 2h2h amplifies noise as the bump decreases. Reusing shocks creates a positive covariance between the two prices and can greatly reduce difference variance.

Var(Δ^h)=Var(V^+)+Var(V^−)−2Cov(V^+,V^−)4h2.\operatorname{Var}(\widehat\Delta_h)=\frac{\operatorname{Var}(\widehat V_+)+\operatorname{Var}(\widehat V_-)-2\operatorname{Cov}(\widehat V_+,\widehat V_-)}{4h^2}.
(59)

Calculate a pathwise bumped difference first and take its average and sample variance. Subtracting two reported standard errors is not an uncertainty calculation. Choose the bump by balancing bias, variance and floating-point sensitivity; an extremely small bump is not automatically more accurate.

Pathwise differentiation

With valid differentiation-under-expectation conditions, differentiate each payoff using the same driving shock. Since ∂ST/∂S0=ST/S0\partial S_T/\partial S_0=S_T/S_0, a European call has the pathwise delta estimator

Δ^PW=1N∑ie−rT𝟙ST(i)>KST(i)S0.\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{PW}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i e^{-rT}\mathbb{1}_{S_T^{(i)}>K}\frac{S_T^{(i)}}{S_0}.
(60)

The probability of hitting the call kink exactly is zero under a continuous distribution, and the first derivative admits this construction. The corresponding pathwise vega observation is

e−rT𝟙ST>KST(TZ−σT).e^{-rT}\mathbb{1}_{S_T>K}S_T(\sqrt T\,Z-\sigma T).
(61)

Vega here is per unit change in volatility, such as from 0.20 to 1.20; divide by 100 to quote sensitivity per one percentage-point volatility move. The standard error is computed from these Greek observations, using paired units if antithetics are applied.

A digital indicator has derivative zero away from its jump, yet its expected payoff changes smoothly with spot. Naively differentiating that indicator gives the wrong delta. Differentiating a pathwise call delta again while ignoring the indicator boundary similarly misses gamma. Payoff discontinuities and boundary terms require smoothing, likelihood ratios or another justified method.

Likelihood-ratio estimators

If a parameter enters the density, differentiation can move to that density. Its derivative divided by the density is the score:

∂θV=𝔼[Hθ(X)∂θlnfθ(X)+∂θHθ(X)].\partial_\theta V=\mathbb{E}\left[H_\theta(X)\,\partial_\theta\ln f_\theta(X)+\partial_\theta H_\theta(X)\right].
(62)

Include discounting within HθH_\theta if it depends on the parameter. For a spot Greek under terminal GBM, the lognormal density score gives

Δ^LR=1N∑iYiZiS0σT.\widehat\Delta_{\mathrm{LR}}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_i Y_i\frac{Z_i}{S_0\sigma\sqrt T}.
(63)

This can handle discontinuous terminal payoffs, but its variance may be larger than pathwise differentiation for a smooth payoff and can be problematic as σT\sigma\sqrt T becomes small. “Unbiased” does not imply “efficient”. Hybrid methods combine conditioning, scores and pathwise derivatives.

Automatic differentiation

Automatic or adjoint differentiation efficiently propagates derivatives through a computational graph while keeping the random inputs fixed. It automates valid pathwise calculations; it does not justify differentiation through a discontinuous exercise decision or barrier indicator. Many-input portfolios can benefit greatly, provided contract nonsmoothness and any regression dependence are handled correctly.

21 / Optimal stopping

American options and least-squares Monte Carlo

European simulation evaluates a known cash flow. American simulation must also determine when exercising is optimal. On a set of exercise dates, the Bermudan value satisfies a backward recursion between immediate payoff and conditional continuation value:

Vj(s)=max(Hj(s),e−r(tj+1−tj)𝔼[Vj+1(Sj+1)|Sj=s]).V_j(s)=\max\left(H_j(s),\ e^{-r(t_{j+1}-t_j)}\mathbb{E}[V_{j+1}(S_{j+1})\mid S_j=s]\right).
(64)

A continuously exercisable American option requires a limiting or suitably refined exercise-time treatment. A fifty-date simulation is a Bermudan approximation, even if it is informally described as an American pricing experiment. With the same model and payoff, additional available exercise dates cannot reduce the true value.

The information constraint

A stopping decision must use information available at that date. Selecting the best exercise date after inspecting the entire realised future path gives a holder perfect foresight. Averaging those maximum path payoffs therefore estimates a different, more valuable claim:

𝔼[maxje−rtjHj(Sj)]≥supτ𝔼[e−rτHτ(Sτ)].\mathbb{E}\left[\max_j e^{-rt_j}H_j(S_j)\right]\ge\sup_\tau\mathbb{E}[e^{-r\tau}H_\tau(S_\tau)].
(65)

Analogy: deciding when to sell without tomorrow's newspaper. A real decision-maker can use today's state and a forecast of future opportunities, but cannot select today's action using tomorrow's realised outcome. A simulation contains tomorrow's outcome in memory; an exercise algorithm must still obey the decision-maker's information boundary.

Least-squares continuation estimates

The Longstaff–Schwartz approach simulates training paths and works backward. At an exercise date, regress future discounted cash flows on basis functions of the current state, usually focusing the exercise comparison on in-the-money paths:

C^j(s)=∑k=0pa^j,kψk(s),a^j=argmina∑i∈Ij(Yi,j−∑kakψk(Si,j))2.\widehat C_j(s)=\sum_{k=0}^{p}\widehat a_{j,k}\psi_k(s),\qquad \widehat a_j=\operatorname{argmin}_{a}\sum_{i\in I_j}\left(Y_{i,j}-\sum_k a_k\psi_k(S_{i,j})\right)^2.
(66)

Here Yi,jY_{i,j} is the cash flow from the currently selected later stopping decision, discounted back to tjt_j; it is not necessarily the payoff at the next date. Compare immediate payoff with fitted continuation, update the selected stopping decision, then move backward.

Scaling states, choosing a stable basis and solving least squares by QR or SVD avoids unnecessarily ill-conditioned normal equations. Higher polynomial degree can overfit, extrapolate badly or become poorly determined where there are few in-the-money paths. A multi-asset or path-dependent option needs a state representation containing the information relevant to future payoffs.

Training versus valuation

Freeze the fitted continuation functions and evaluate the resulting exercise policy on independent paths in a forward pass. At each date, the policy uses only the state observed at that date. The average discounted payoff of this policy is unbiased conditional on the trained policy and is bounded above in expectation by the true Bermudan optimum.

The estimated policy value can exceed the true optimum in a finite sample because of sampling noise. A confidence interval around the held-out estimate quantifies its simulation uncertainty conditional on the policy. It does not automatically include policy suboptimality, training variation, insufficient state variables or exercise-grid error. In-sample valuation can suffer look-ahead effects and should not be treated as an independently validated lower bound.

Upper bounds and convergence checks

Dual constructions can obtain upper bounds from valid martingales. For a discounted payoff process and a martingale MjM_j with M0=0M_0=0, the expected maximum of discounted payoff minus MjM_j is an upper bound. Implementing such a construction requires preserving the martingale condition; subtracting an arbitrary fitted continuation process is insufficient.

Useful diagnostics vary the number of training and evaluation paths, basis complexity and exercise dates separately. Compare a vanilla put against a converged lattice benchmark, and separate changes in policy value from noise in its held-out evaluation. The detailed original algorithm and primal–dual development are linked in the references.

22 / Interpretation

Validation, efficiency and model risk

A useful Monte Carlo result is an estimate whose target, sampling design and limitations can be explained. Numerical validation establishes that the estimator represents the specified model and contract; it does not establish that the model describes every market feature.

Financial invariants and known limits

For European vanilla GBM, compare prices against Black–Scholes across in-, at- and out-of-the-money strikes, several maturities, yields and volatilities. Validate zero maturity and zero volatility explicitly. Check discounted-stock means against S0e−qTS_0e^{-qT}, with their own uncertainty, and verify sample-level put–call parity using the actual simulated stock mean.

With the same terminal stock scenarios and otherwise identical call conventions, increasing strike cannot increase any path payoff. The resulting sample price curve is decreasing and convex in strike. Repricing each strike with independent shocks obscures those pathwise properties with unrelated noise; common scenarios give stronger diagnostics.

Statistical calibration

Across independent repeated runs, examine bias, RMSE and interval coverage against known truth. A nominal 95% interval need not contain the benchmark in every run. Conversely, choosing or publishing only seeds whose intervals contain the benchmark turns a validation experiment into selection on the result.

For antithetics, verify pair-unit accounting. For controls, verify the exact expected control and independent coefficient fit. For importance sampling, verify density ratios and weighted-payoff moments. For RQMC, use independent scramble means. For LSM, separate training from evaluation and interpret the interval as conditional policy uncertainty.

Where uncertainty can remain

Different error sources require different checks
SourceTypical remedy or diagnostic
Sampling variationMore independent units or a more efficient estimator
Time-scheme biasCoupled mesh refinement or exact transitions
Unresolved continuous monitoringCorrect conditional crossing or extrema treatment
Exercise-policy approximationRicher validated policies and lower/upper bounds
Parameter uncertaintyCalibration uncertainty and parameter sensitivity analysis
Model inadequacyAlternative models and economically relevant comparisons
Contract convention mismatchCorrect fixing, exercise and settlement specification

These errors are not all independent and cannot always be added as simple standard deviations. A confidence interval from payoff sampling measures only the component justified by its construction. Naming the unresolved component is more informative than printing extra decimals.

Precision and performance

Evaluate variance reduction at equal work and include its pilot or setup cost. A more elaborate method can lose at small budgets and win at larger budgets. Memory use, batching, vectorisation and hardware affect performance; benchmark the actual contract rather than a random-number loop in isolation.

Parallelism speeds calculations but does not repair a wrong payoff or dependence structure. A robust ordering of work is to define the target, simplify it mathematically, validate a transparent estimator, then improve variance and execution speed. Validation cases should remain available after optimisation.

23 / Interactive study

Interactive simulation laboratory

Run exact terminal GBM simulations for a European call or put. Change the contract and model inputs, the production payoff budget and the seed. The estimator can use plain sampling, antithetic pairs, an independently fitted discounted-stock control, or their combination.

The displayed path budget counts production payoff evaluations. Antithetic methods have half as many independent units. Controlled methods additionally use a separate 1,024-unit pilot: 1,024 payoff evaluations for a plain control, or 2,048 for a paired control. Its coefficient is frozen before production; the pilot is excluded from the price and included in the reported total work.

European Monte Carlo laboratoryExact terminal GBM / seeded simulation

Paired methods require an even budget. Controlled methods add separate pilot work.

Suggested experiments

Start with the benchmark and compare methods at 20,000 production payoff evaluations. The realised absolute error may be smaller for a less efficient method by chance; the standard error and repeated runs describe reliability. Repeat the same method with several seeds, then increase the budget by a factor of four and compare typical interval widths.

Raise the strike to 180 for a call and reduce the budget. Notice how rare exercise can destabilise plain sampling and how an all-zero sample can create an uninformative zero-width interval. The laboratory flags that condition; it does not implement importance sampling for every parameter choice. The separate rare-event chapter provides the weighted construction.

Set volatility or maturity to zero to inspect deterministic limits. Add a continuous yield and check the control expectation S0e−qTS_0e^{-qT}. Compare call and put control signs. All running intervals are pointwise normal approximations; their sequence is an explanatory plot, not a sequential stopping guarantee.
